title: Collusion-Resistant Constrained PRFs for Compute-&-Compare Predicates from LWE
abstract:
We design the first collusion-resistant constrained PRFs (CPRFs) for a non-trivial and expressive class of constraints from standard LWE. The two predicate classes for which we design CPRFs are: compute-&-compare and predicated range constraints. We improve our CPRF for compute-&-compare predicates to also satisfy collusion-resistant constraint privacy. An additional feature of our CPRFs is that they also satisfy (almost-)key-homomorphic property. Prior to this work, we did not have any post-quantum collusion-resistant CPRF beyond prefixfixing constraints, and collusion-resistant CPRFs for expressive predicates relied on either code obfuscation or multilinear maps.

As an immediate application, we obtain a two-sided predicate encryption (PE) and functional encryption (FE) for the compute-&-compare class in the symmetric-key setting. Prior to this work, we did not have any post-quantum construction for 2-sided PE/FE beyond inner product predicates. An important contribution of this work is to introduce a new framework of purifying functionality. The main motivation behind our new framework is to systematically eliminate zeroizing attacks, which have been a highly successful cryptanalysis paradigm for breaking various candidates for advanced cryptographic objects.

                                                   Abstract
            We design the first collusion-resistant constrained PRFs (CPRFs) for a non-trivial and
        expressive class of constraints from standard LWE. The two predicate classes for which we
        design CPRFs are: compute-&-compare and predicated range constraints. We improve our
        CPRF for compute-&-compare predicates to also satisfy collusion-resistant constraint privacy.
        An additional feature of our CPRFs is that they also satisfy (almost-)key-homomorphic property.
        Prior to this work, we did not have any post-quantum collusion-resistant CPRF beyond prefix-
        fixing constraints, and collusion-resistant CPRFs for expressive predicates relied on either code
        obfuscation or multilinear maps.
            As an immediate application, we obtain a two-sided predicate encryption (PE) and functional
        encryption (FE) for the compute-&-compare class in the symmetric-key setting. Prior to this
        work, we did not have any post-quantum construction for 2-sided PE/FE beyond inner product
        predicates. An important contribution of this work is to introduce a new framework of purifying
        functionality. The main motivation behind our new framework is to systematically eliminate
        zeroizing attacks, which have been a highly successful cryptanalysis paradigm for breaking
        various candidates for advanced cryptographic objects.

1        Introduction
Constrained pseudorandom functions [BW13, BGI14, KPTZ13] (CPRFs) are a powerful advance-
ment of pseudorandom functions (PRFs) [GGM86]. Syntactically, a CPRF is defined nearly identi-
cal to a standard PRF, as in it has a Setup algorithm that takes a security parameter λ, and outputs
the (master) PRF key K, and an Eval algorithm that takes K and input x, and outputs the PRF
value FK (x). The crucial difference between traditional and constrained PRFs is that CPRFs have
another special algorithm, Constrain. The Constrain algorithm takes as input, the master key K
and a boolean predicate ϕ, and outputs a “constrained” key, Kϕ . The desired functionality from
Kϕ is that one can compute the PRF output FK (x) on any x as long as x satisfies the predicate ϕ
(i.e., ϕ(x) = 1), yet K is independent of ϕ as one wants to chose ϕ dynamically, after setup.
Pseudorandomness. A critical feature for CPRFs is their ability to maintain pseudorandomness
even under a collusion attack. This is formalized as constrained pseudorandomness property. It
guarantees that any polytime adversary that corrupts a group of constrained keys Kϕ1 , . . . , KϕQ ,
for Q predicates {ϕi }i , cannot distinguish the PRF output on a point x∗ as long as none of the
predicates satisfy it. Here Q denotes the collusion size, and CPRF is said to be collusion-resistant
if Q can be any polynomial.
Privacy. Another crucial property for CPRFs is that of constraint privacy [BGI14, KPTZ13,
BLW17]. It states an adversary cannot learn any non-trivial information about the predicates
{ϕi }i from a set of constrained keys {Kϕi }i . The notion of non-trivial information has to be
defined carefully as the attacker can pick an input x, use every constrained key to evaluate on x,
and compare the resulting outputs to learn which constraints satisfy x [BLW17].
Current state of affairs. Despite a decade of intensive study, achieving collusion-resistant CPRFs
for general predicates remains a formidable challenge. Without leveraging heavy cryptographic
machinery (such as indistinguishability obfuscation [BGI+ 01], multilinear maps [BS02, GGH13a,
CLT15, GGH15]), our ability to construct collusion-resistant schemes is remarkably limited. Even
when constraint privacy is not a requirement, existing collusion-resistant CPRFs are restricted to a
narrow class of functions: specifically, prefix-fixing constraints [GGM86, BW13, BGI14]1 and left-
right predicates [BW13]2 . Neither class provides the expressivity required to support the diverse
array of applications envisioned for constrained pseudorandomness. Moreover, if one desires post-
quantum security, the landscape narrows further; only prefix-fixing PRFs are currently known, as
they follow directly from the seminal Goldreich-Goldwasser-Micali (GGM) construction [GGM86,
BW13, BGI14].
    More remarkably, designing CPRFs does not get easier even against a ‘fixed’ collusion size [DKXY02,
SS10, GLW12, GVW12]. In the fixed collusion setting, Q is a-priori fixed during setup and security
is only guaranteed if no more than Q keys get corrupted. For most primitives, such as encryption,
signatures, and even certain forms of obfuscation, restricting to bounded collusion security makes
the problem much easier [DKXY02, SS10, GLW12, GVW12, GKP+ 13]. In sharp contrast, CPRFs
supporting a small (e.g., two) number of corrupted keys remain elusive to this day. All prior CPRFs
that go beyond inner-product predicates can either resist a single collusion (i.e., Q = 1), or require
obfuscation [BW13, KPTZ13, BGI14, BV15, DKW16, CC17, BTVW17, BKW17, BKM17, PS18,

Why are CPRFs so hard to design? On a fundamental level, this large schism between
CPRFs and other advanced primitives stems from the fact that CPRFs implicitly enforce a stronger
consistency property. Two constrained keys for a CPRF must output identical PRF values on
a common satisfying input. For other advanced primitives, this consistency property is not as
stringent. As an example, consider attribute-based encryption (ABE) [SW05, GPSW06] where two
predicate keys only need to recover the plaintext from a ciphertext and nothing else.
    This strong consistency requirement raises the technical difficulty in designing CPRFs, which
brings us to the central question that we study:

      Q1. Can we design collusion-resistant CPRFs from standard assumptions for any class of
                 constraint predicates that cannot be captured as inner-products?

Additionally, we ask:

Q2. Can we design collusion-resistant CPRFs with constraint privacy for any non-trivial class of
                            predicates from standard assumptions?

As two-key constraint privacy for general circuits is known to imply obfuscation [CC17], thus
one must carefully delineate a non-trivial class of predicates that provides meaningful expressivity
without inadvertently collapsing into the regime of obfuscation.

1.1     Our Results
In this work, we give positive answers to both questions, Q1 and Q2, while emphasizing on realizing
post-quantum security. We give the first post-quantum collusion-resistant CPRF, that goes beyond
prefix-fixing [GGM86, BW13, BGI14], and also prove it to be constraint private. As a direct
application of our CPRFs, we give the first post-quantum collusion-resistant 2-sided PE for a non-
trivial class of predicates. A key technical contribution of this work is a new framework, that we call
Purified Circuit Class framework, to eliminate susceptibility to zeroizing attacks [CLT14, CHL+ 14,
CGH+ 15, BGH+ 15, BBKK18, CVW18b, AP20, HJL21, JLLS23] in the context of lattice-based
CPRFs. Below we summarize our key results:

  1. Collusion-Resistant Constraint-Private CPRF for compute-&-compare predicates
     from LWE. We construct a CPRF for compute-&-compare predicates (i.e., equality testing
     on function output). Each constraint predicate CC[f, y] is associated with a ‘compute’ func-
     tion f (that can be represented by a polynomial-sized circuit) and a function output y. A
     CPRF key for CC[f, y] can be used to evaluate the PRF on any input x as long as f (x) = y.
       We prove our CPRF satisfies collusion-resistant constrained pseudorandomness and constraint
       privacy, under the Learning With Errors (LWE) assumption [Reg05], as long as the attacker
       corrupts constrained keys for the same compute function f but many different comparison
       points y1 , . . . , yQ . Prior CPRFs were secure as long as an attacker gets at most one constrained
       key and, as we demonstrate in this work, prior lattice-based CPRFs can be easily broken if we
       corrupt just two keys for compute-&-compare predicates, even with same compute function
       f and two distinct comparison points.



                                                     2
  2. Collusion-Resistant CPRFs for predicated range from LWE. We generalize our main
     CPRF construction to support predicated range constraints (i.e., range checking on function
     output). Each constraint predicate CC[f, y, z] is associated with a ‘compute’ function f and
     an output range [y, z], where an input x satisfies the predicate if f (x) ∈ [y, z]. We prove
     our CPRF for predicated range satisfies collusion-resistant constrained pseudorandomness as
     long as the ranges are pairwise disjoint. We leave it as an interesting open question to prove
     constraint privacy for this constraint class.

  3. 2-Sided Predicate Encryption. As a direct application of our CPRFs, we construct a
     collusion-resistant 2-sided (or strongly attribute-hiding) predicate encryption (PE) scheme [BW07,
     KSW08, GKW17a] for compute-&-compare predicates under standard LWE. Our encryption
     system is a symmetric-key scheme and also satisfies predicate privacy (i.e., decryption keys
     hide the predicate). Prior to this work, 2-sided PE could only be built for inner-product
     predicates [BW07, KSW08], or by invoking obfuscation and related primitives [GGH+ 13b,
     SW14, ABSV15].

Key-Homomorphism: an added benefit. Our CPRF constructions also satisfy (almost-)key-homomorphic
property w.r.t. the master key as well as constrained keys [BLMR13, BFP+ 15, CVW+ 18a, GQWW19].
Briefly, (almost-)key-homomorphism states that FK1 (x) + FK2 (x) ≈ FK1 +K2 (x), where K1 , K2
are two master keys or two constrained keys for the same predicate. The key-homomorphism
property has proven to be extremely valuable for a variety for applications [BLMR13, BFP+ 15,
CVW+ 18a, GQWW19] and, to the best of our knowledge, we did not have any collusion-resistant
key-homomorphic CPRF for any predicate other than prefix-fixing predicates from standard as-
sumptions.

1.2   Applications
Our construction of a symmetric-key 2-sided PE scheme yields significant implications. Notably,
this PE scheme inherently provides symmetric-key function-hiding functional encryption (FE) [SSW09,
GKP+ 13, AAB+ 15] for the same class. Below, we outline several key applications.
Searchable and Order-Revealing Encryption. Searchable Symmetric Encryption (SSE) and
Order-Revealing/Preserving Encryption (ORE/OPE) enable efficient querying over encrypted databases [SWP00,
Goh03, AKSX04, CGKO06, BCLO09, CK10, BCO11, BLR+ 15]. Our 2-sided PE for compute-
&-compare allows for secure sorting and searching while maintaining attribute hiding even for
successful queries.
    Consider an organization hosting employee records on a third-party cloud. The organization can
delegate the ability to retrieve records within a specific salary interval [t, 2t] or identify employees
in a specific location. By utilizing our 2-sided security, the cloud server can execute these queries
without learning the underlying salary values or geographical data, even for the records that match
the query criteria.
Watermarkable and Traceable Constrained PRFs. Watermarkable [HMW07, BGI+ 01,
CHN+ 16] and traceable PRFs [GKWW21] allow a master authority to embed and detect “wa-
termarks” within secret keys to prevent unauthorized distribution or misuse. These are vital for
challenge-response authentication and traitor tracing.
    Existing schemes primarily support watermarking the master PRF key, which is insufficient
for systems requiring fine-grained access control (e.g., identity-based traitor tracing [NWZ16,


                                                3
GKW18]). By leveraging our collusion-resistant CPRFs with constraint privacy, one can design
watermarkable constrained keys. This allows an authority to delegate restricted PRF capabilities
while retaining the ability to trace the specific constrained key used in a leak or misuse.
Collusion-Resistant Private Constrained MACs. Private constrained MACs [BGI14, BLW17]—the
symmetric analogue of constrained signatures—allow a master key holder to delegate the ability to
tag messages that satisfy a specific predicate. Applications include enforcing departmental spend-
ing limits or delegating university purchase authorizations without revealing the underlying policy
or employee credentials.
    Prior constructions based on 1-key private CPRFs were limited to single-user security. Our
results directly enable collusion-resistant private constrained MACs, allowing multiple delegated
users to operate simultaneously without compromising the privacy of the organizational policies or
the security of the tagging mechanism.
Fraud and Threat Detection. Our framework naturally supports “investigative” encryption
models [BW07, SBC+ 07, GVW15], such as credit card fraud detection or suspicious content filter-
ing. In these scenarios:

   • Fraud Investigation: Investigators can get keys to identify transactions with specific fraudu-
     lent signatures (e.g., target ranges or specific metadata matches).
   • Threat Detection: Cloud providers can host keys that trigger alerts for suspicious keywords
     or communication patterns.

Since the desired functionality can be naturally implemented as compute-&-compare and predicated
range policies, thus the use of 2-sided PE ensures that the sensitive details of the transaction or
communication remain hidden from the investigator until a a “suspicious” item is flagged.
Beyond the specific applications discussed, the collusion-resistance and key-homomorphism proper-
ties of our construction offer broader utility in the design of advanced lattice-based primitives. Key-
homomorphic CPRFs have played an important role in traitor tracing [CFN94, GKW18, CVW+ 18a]
and trace-and-revoke systems [NP01, GQWW19]. By providing the first collusion-resistant real-
ization for compute-&-compare and predicated range classes, our work effectively removes the
‘single-key barrier’ that has limited applications. We expect this framework to inspire new research
into achieving collusion resistance for even more expressive, possible non-purified circuit classes
under standard lattice assumptions.

1.3   Related work
The concept of CPRFs was concurrently introduced by Boneh and Waters, Boyle et al., and Ki-
ayias et al. [BW13, BGI14, KPTZ13]. They observed that the GGM construction [GGM86] in-
herently provides a CPRF for prefix-fixing predicates under the minimal assumption of one-way
functions (OWFs). Since the work of Sahai and Waters [SW14], puncturable PRFs have become a
fundamental tool in applications of indistinguishability obfuscation (iO). Broadly, existing CPRF
constructions can be categorized by their underlying cryptographic techniques: obfuscation-based,
lattice-based, group-based, and combinatorial approaches.
Obfuscation-Based Constructions. Using iO or related “heavy hammers,” several constructions
achieve collusion-resistant CPRFs for all circuits and even Turing machines [DKW16, BLW17,
BKW17]. Some of these schemes [BKW17, BLW17] also achieve collusion-resistant constraint

privacy. While expressive, these constructions rely on the existence of iO, making them less suitable
for deployment under standard, well-studied assumptions like LWE.
Lattice-Based Constructions. Under standard lattice assumptions, numerous constructions
exist for general circuits [BV15, BKM17, CC17, BTVW17]. Several of these have been extended
to provide 1-key constraint privacy. However, a significant limitation persists: all current lattice-
based templates are restricted to single-key security. As discussed in our technical overview, these
algebraic structures (e.g., BGG+ or GGH) are inherently vulnerable to key-subtraction or mix-and-
match attacks when more than one key is issued.
Group-Based Constructions. In the random oracle model (ROM), Boneh and Waters [BW13]
designed collusion-resistant CPRFs for left-right constraints using bilinear maps. Subsequent
works [GHKW17, Bit17, AMN+ 18] achieved 1-key security for substring and NC1 predicates under
DDH-hard groups. More recently, Ishai et al. [ILL24] designed 1-key CPRFs for general constraints
based on DCR or DDH with small-exponent assumptions. While recent works [CMPR23, BMO+ 25]
have explored 1-key private CPRFs for inner-product predicates, none of these group-based schemes
(save for the specialized ROM construction in [BW13]) support more than one key corruption or
satisfy constraint privacy for general classes.
Combinatorial Approaches. A final direction involves restricting the predicate class to in-
ner products or O(1)-CNFs and leveraging combinatorial techniques [Tsa19, DKN+ 20, CDD+ 24].
While these approaches utilize mild assumptions (e.g., OWFs), they are subject to a “combinatorial
explosion” regarding corruption sets; for instance, the scheme of Davidson et al. [DKN+ 20] resists
only O(1) corruptions. These methods appear fundamentally limited and unlikely to generalize to
general constraints or full collusion resistance.
Summary. Prior to this work, the landscape of CPRFs was divided between iO-based schemes
(which provide full collusion resistance for all circuits) and standard-assumption schemes (which
are almost exclusively limited to single-key security). Our work bridges this gap, providing the first
collusion-resistant CPRFs with constraint privacy from standard lattice assumptions for meaningful
predicate classes.

Looking ahead. Over the last few years, numerous works have proposed new non-standard (and
even non-falsifiable) lattice assumptions [Wee22, Tsa22, VWW22, WWW22, ARYY23, HLL23,
Wee24, HLL24, AKY24, Wee25, HLL25] to go beyond established barriers in lattice-based cryp-
tography. This has had mixed success. While relying on these non-standard assumptions led to
the first provable designs for many advanced primitives [Wee22, Tsa22, VWW22, Wee24, HLL24,
Wee25, HLL25] for which we do not yet have any constructions under standard lattice assumptions,
their foundations have not resisted cryptanalysis [AMYY25, HHY25, DJM+ 25, BÜW24, HJL25].
Although recent works have made important progress towards the goal of lattice-based (post-
quantum) functional cryptography, we believe a paradigm shift is essential in the community’s
approach in order to design advanced primitives while reducing to standard LWE.
    Taking a step back, we view our results as proposing a new avenue for bypassing zeroizing attacks
in lattice-based cryptography. Such attacks have been a consistent source of successful cryptanalytic
strategies on various lattice-based candidates. We believe that our purification framework could
be widely applicable across other primitives in lattice-based cryptography to design new schemes
with provable security under standard LWE.


2    Technical Overview
We start with the key technical barrier that deters realizing collusion-resistant CPRFs for circuits
from lattices.
Zeroizing attacks: a key technical barrier. Zeroizing attacks are a powerful methodology to
cryptanalyze candidates for advanced cryptographic objects [CLT14, CHL+ 14, CGH+ 15, BGH+ 15,
BBKK18, CVW18b, AP20, HJL21, JLLS23]. Abstractly, a zeroizing (colluding) attacker in CPRFs
works as follows: (1) corrupt two (or more) constrained keys, (2) evaluate them on an input x
that satisfies all constraints (which must give the same output by CPRF correctness), and (3)
algebraically combine these keys and outputs, and extract non-trivial (secret) encodings of ‘zero’.
    Step (3) is the most crucial step and it reveals non-trivial information about the PRF master
key msk in the lattice setting. Basically, each PRF output non-trivially depends on msk, and if
two constrained keys can evaluate the PRF on a common point, then they can be used to learn
the same msk encoding in two different ways. In lattice-based CPRFs, being able to compute the
same encoding of msk in two different ways leaks underlying errors, eventually breaking pseudoran-
domness. Therefore, all prior lattice-based CPRFs [BV15, BTVW17, CC17, CVW18b, BKM17]
succumb to zeroizing attacks. Since zeroizing attacks require at least two keys, thus prior works
could prove 1-key constrained pseudorandomness, but fell apart when an attacker corrupts even
two.
    Our goal is to allow an arbitrary number of key corruptions, while avoiding zeroizing attacks.
Towards that goal, we introduce a new notion that we call ‘purified circuit classes’ to eliminate
susceptibility to zeroizing attacks.
“Purifying” Functionality: Eliminating Zeroizing Attacks. Our starting observation is that
the abstract zeroizing attack methodology no longer works if an attacker corrupts constraint keys
that do not have an overlapping support. Let Cb be a class of predicates where every pair (distinct)
predicates have a disjoint support. That is, ∀C ̸= C ′ ∈ C,

    We call such a predicate class, C,
                                    b to be a purified constraint class. Intuitively, this enforces zero
overlap between constraints. Essentially, each constrained key skC controls a unique and disjoint
partition of the input space. Our intuition is that if attacker can only acquire secret keys that

correspond to a purified class, then zeroizing attack methodology might not work. Basically, the
abstract zeroizing attack template stops at step (2) when an adversary cannot evaluate two keys
on the same point anymore.
    Naturally, moving to this framework invites three fundamental questions:
Q1 (Utility): Are there meaningful predicate classes that reside within this ‘purified’ regime?

Q2 (Complexity): Does the restriction to purified classes render the construction of collusion-
    resistant CPRFs trivial?

Q3 (Gap Analysis): Are existing lattice-based CPRFs already implicitly secure for such classes,
    or can we identify concrete vulnerabilities?
In the following, we address each of these in turn.
Addressing Q1: The Existence of Expressive Purified Predicates. We answer in the
affirmative by identifying two significant and expressive families of purified predicates.
I. compute-&-Compare Predicates. Our first example is the class of compute-&-compare circuits.
Informally, each circuit in this family checks whether a function f maps an input x to a target
value y. Formally, for a function f : X → Y and a target y ∈ Y, we define the circuit Cf,y such
that:
                                     Cf,y (x) = 1 ⇐⇒ f (x) = y
For a given f , any collection of circuits F ⊆ {Cf,y : y ∈ Y} constitutes a compute-&-compare class.
Notably, any such class is inherently purified: for any two distinct targets y ̸= y ′ , the supports of
Cf,y and Cf,y′ are disjoint as f is a function (i.e., supp(Cf,y ) ∩ supp(Cf,y′ ) = ∅).
II. Predicated Range Constraints. We further generalize this to the predicated range class. Here,
the constraint is satisfied if the function output falls within a specific interval. For a function f ,
we define the range circuit Cf,[y,z] as:

                                   Cf,[y,z] (x) = 1 ⇐⇒ y ≤ f (x) ≤ z

A collection of such circuits {Cf,[yi ,zi ] } is a purified predicated range class provided the correspond-
ing intervals [yi , zi ] in the co-domain Y are pairwise non-overlapping. This class offers a powerful
generalization, allowing for delegated evaluation over partitioned sub-domains of the function’s
range.
    These predicates have been studied in the context of code obfuscation [GKW17b, WZ17] and are
fairly common in the searchable symmetric encryption (SSE) literature [AKSX04, BCLO09, BCO11,
BLR+ 15]. We refer the reader to Section 1.2 for a detailed discussion on potential applications.
Addressing Q2: The Non-Triviality of Purified Constraints. The reader might be won-
dering: does restricting the predicate class to disjoint supports (the “purified” regime) render the
construction of collusion-resistant CPRFs trivial? One might consider a naive approach that par-
titions the input space X according to the constraints and assigns independent PRF keys to each
partition—for instance, defining Eval(msk, x) = F (Kpartition(x) , x).
    However, such an approach fails to satisfy the fundamental requirement of a CPRF: independence of core PRF fu
In a standard CPRF, the Setup and Eval algorithms must remain independent of the specific con-
straint issued. The master key msk defines a single, consistent pseudorandom function over the
entire domain {0, 1}n , whereas constraints can be selected dynamically via the Constrain algorithm
later. A partition-based approach would require “fixing” the constraint (e.g., the function f in a

                                                    7
compute-&-compare class) during the Setup phase. This would yield a constraint-specific CPRF
rather than a general-purpose CPRF. Our construction maintains a single msk capable of issu-
ing keys for any predicate in the class (and for arbitrary functions f ) without requiring apriori
knowledge of these constraints at setup time.
     We emphasize that the requirement of Setup and Eval being independent of the constraining
predicates is essential for nearly all applications as well as it ensures the problem does not become
trivial. In particular, designing CPRFs even for general constraints (i.e., without the purified
restriction) is relatively straightforward if the Setup or Eval algorithm knows the set of constraints
C1 , . . . , CQ for which a key will be generated. The idea is simple: partition the input space into
2Q disjoint regions based on the validity vector y ∈ {0, 1}n of the input x against the constraints
(where y[i] = Ci (x)). The system simply assigns an independent standard PRF key Ky for each
possible vector y, and a constrained key for Ci corresponds to {Ky } for all y such that y[i] = 1. For
completeness, we provide this simple construction for CPRFs in this so-called “static-constraint”
model in Section 10.
Addressing Q3: The Failure of Existing Lattice-Based CPRFs. With the introduction
of purified circuits, it is natural to ask whether existing lattice-based CPRFs [BV15, BTVW17,
BKM17, CC17, CVW+ 18a] already satisfy collusion resistance when restricted to such classes.
We answer this in the negative. We examine the two dominant algebraic paradigms—the BGG+
approach and the GGH approach—and demonstrate that both are fundamentally insecure against
collusion, even in the purified setting.
I. Vulnerability of the BGG+ Approach. The constructions in [BV15, BTVW17, BKM17] utilize
the homomorphic properties of the BGG+ framework [BGG+ 14]. In these schemes, the constrained
key for a function f is typically an encoding of the form:

                                    skf := sT · (B − f ⊗ G) + e

where s is the LWE secret (serving as the PRF seed), B is a public matrix, and G is the gadget
matrix. Correctness relies on the fact that for any x such that f (x) = 0, one can homomorphically
derive sT (B · Hx ) ≈ Eval(msk, x).
The Attack: This design collapses under collusion for the compute-&-Compare class. Consider
an adversary who obtains two keys sky0 and sky1 for the same function f but distinct targets y0 , y1 .
The keys take the form:
                                    skyi ≈ sT · (B − [f | yi ] ⊗ G)
By simply computing the difference sky0 − sky1 , the sT B and f -dependent terms cancel out, leaving
a term of the form sT · ((y1 − y0 ) ⊗ G) + e′ . Since y0 ̸= y1 , the adversary can use the gadget
structure of G to recover the LWE secret s in its entirety. This total break of the master secret
key demonstrates that the BGG+ framework cannot natively support collusion resistance.
II. Vulnerability of the GGH Approach. The second paradigm, based on GGH-style encodings [GGH15],
constructs CPRFs for log-depth or log-space circuits using chains of matrices [CC17, CVW18b].
Here, the constrained key is a sequence of “links” that allow evaluation only if the input x traverses
a valid path in a branching program.
The Attack: These constructions are susceptible to a mix-and-match attack. Even in the purified
setting (e.g., bit-fixing constraints), an adversary holding keys for two disjoint constraints can
“splice” the matrix chains together. For example, by combining the first half of a chain from Key
A with the second half of Key B, the adversary can evaluate the PRF on inputs that satisfy neither


                                                  8
constraint. While this attack can be mitigated for single-key security, the algebraic structure of
the GGH encodings inherently allows for the recombination of chain segments across multiple keys,
effectively breaking collusion resistance.
The vulnerabilities identified in these two templates reveal a fundamental gap: existing lattice-
based CPRFs are susceptible to direct algebraic breaks, even when the adversary is restricted to a
purified class of constraints. This demonstrates that existing techniques are insufficient for achieving
collusion resistance in this regime. Our construction addresses this gap by effectively immunizing
constrained keys against “algebraic combination” attacks. We achieve this by expanding the lattice-
based encodings and leveraging the inherent structure of the compute-&-compare and predicated
range classes.

2.1   Achieving collusion-resistance for compute-&-compare
We first describe a baseline design that captures the main idea of our approach: algebraically
decoupling the function description from the output value by introducing an explicit offset term
that depends only on the target output. In the standard BGG+ instantiations for compute-&-
compare, the target y is embedded directly into the homomorphic evaluation path (e.g., encoding
the circuit Cf,y such that Cf,y (x) = 1 if only if f (x) = y).
    Our first idea is to sample a fresh random matrix {Ay }y for each distinct target value. Given
this matrix, we will keep the BGG+ encoding dependent on f only, and move target dependence
into a separate offset. A direct way to enforce this is to represent constrained evaluation as a shifted
version of master key evaluation:

                               (B − f T ⊗ G) · HUx,f = B · HUx − Af (x) ,

where Af (x) is an offset family indexed by the output of target function f on input x. For a
constrained key for function f and target y, the first component remains the standard BGG+ term

not just unpredictable. So the baseline constrained evaluation is exactly the master key evaluation
minus the offset indexed by f (x). To ensure this offset can be canceled whenever the target
matches, we give out a target-specific correction term as the second component of the constrained

If f (x) = y, then Ay = Af (x) , so the residual offset vanishes and we recover the master evaluation

pseudorandomness attack. This is due the fact that Ay is randomly sampled for each target value
y, thus looks like an LWE sample.
    This separation is the key structural feature that enables many constrained keys for one fixed
function without re-encoding targets in the shared BGG+ part. The above design relies on the
matrix-valued homomorphic evaluation: the universal circuit Ux is defined to generate the matrix
output, namely Ux (f ) = Af (x) . We remark that the matrix-valued homomorphic evaluation was
originally developed in the context of proving constraint privacy for 1-key CPRFs [BTVW17], while
we use it for homomorphically computing a ‘computation-dependent’ offset.
Handling inefficiency of Setup. In the baseline approach, Setup samples an independent random
public matrix Ay for every y ∈ Y, and the constrained key for target y includes the noisy linear term
sT Ay + noise. While sampling each Ay matrix randomly substantially helps in proving collusion-
resistant constrained pseudorandomness, it makes the CPRF system to be highly inefficient. Note
that the universal circuit Ux is effectively defined with this table hardwired (as this circuit must
know which of the offset matrices need to added). Therefore, both parameter size and representation
complexity scale with |Y|. Effectively, when |Y| is exponential, this system becomes infeasible.
Thus, we would need the number of targets |Y| to be polynomially bounded. This is a severe
restriction that we would like to avoid.
    To remove this bottleneck, we keep exactly the same offset-correction structure and replace
only how Ay is generated. Instead of hardwiring an explicit table {Ay }y∈Y in pp, we instantiate
Ay using the matrix-generation framework of any of the prior key-homomorphic PRF works such
as [BLMR13, BP14]. In this approach, Ay is efficiently computable from y via a recursive or
sequential gadget-based composition, so setup no longer needs to publish one fresh random matrix
per target value. The constrained key still contains the same target handle sT Ay + noisey , and
constrained evaluation is unchanged at the algebraic level. Hence correctness continues to follow
from the same offset cancellation argument.
    This replacement preserves the pseudorandomness argument as well. From the adversary’s view,
each target handle remains an LWE sample indexed by the queried target.           So for polynomially
many queries, the joint distribution sT B + noise, sT Ayi + noiseyi }i∈[Q] is still pseudorandom un-

der LWE. Therefore we keep the same collusion-resistant security intuition while eliminating the
explicit |Y|-size public table.
    We point out that the above construction naturally satisfies key-homomorphism property for,
both, master keys as well as constrained keys. Key-homomorphism for master key follows the same
argument as many prior works [BLMR13, BP14], which is the PRF computation is affine in the
master secret key. For key-homomorphism of constrained keys, we can again rely on the same affine
property as well as the fact that public-offset matrix Ay will be common across different systems.

2.2   Constraint privacy for compute-&-compare predicates
Our next goal is to also achieve constraint privacy for our compute-&-compare CPRF scheme.
Observe that our previous construction already hides the target value y in each constrained key.
In particular, the target-specific component is sT Ay + noisey , which is an LWE sample and is
computationally indistinguishable from random. So the constrained key does not directly reveal
the target value. However, this is not sufficient for constraint privacy. The evaluation algorithm still

                                                  10
requires the compute function f to compute HUx,f , so f must effectively be given to the evaluator.
Clearly, this is not constraint private anymore.
    To hide f , we follow the template of [GVW15, BTVW17] and encrypt f under homomorphic
encryption (HE) [GSW13]. At a high level, we replace the plaintext evaluation of f with homo-
morphic evaluation on a ciphertext ct = Enc(f ), while reusing the same LWE secret s in both
the BGG+ layer and the HE layer. This secret reuse is the standard mechanism that allows the
evaluator to combine homomorphic output with the constrained-key term and recover the correct
value without learning the underlying circuit.
    Our setting requires one additional modification. Prior boolean templates rely on decryption
of a bit that directly cancels the gap between constrained and master evaluation. In our construc-
tion, that gap is matrix-valued and equals the offset indexed by f (x). So we extend the GSW
homomorphic evaluation to matrix outputs as well. Let Ux be the universal circuit with output
Af (x) , and let MtrxEval(Ux , ct) denote homomorphic matrix evaluation on encrypted f . We use
AllButLastRow and LastRow for the top and bottom parts of this evaluated ciphertext, respectively.
The constrained key is

Adaptive security in the ROM. Our standard-model proof establishes selective security, where
the adversary commits to the relevant compute function before the public parameters are gener-
ated. This restriction can be removed in the random oracle model by the standard output-hashing
transformation. The variant keeps the same constrained keys and the same algebraic evaluation
procedure, but replaces the final output zx by H(zx ). For an admissible challenge input x⋆ , the
underlying value zx⋆ remains hidden from the adversary by the security of the base construction.
Thus, except with negligible probability, the adversary never queries zx⋆ to the random oracle.
Conditioned on this event, H(zx⋆ ) is a fresh random string, and the simulator may program this
value as the challenge output. This gives the usual adaptive security upgrade in the ROM, following
[AMN+ 18].

2.3   CPRFs for predicated range constraints
Next, we generalize our base CPRF construction for compute-&-compare to the class of predicated
range circuits. At a high level, our plan is to combine our base CPRF construction with the prefix-
fixing CRPF based on GGM [GGM86] PRFs. Essentially, our idea is to ensure that the user of
the constrained keys can do partial evaluation over the tree instead of only given the leaf vectors.
More concretely, given sT · Ay + noise as part of the constrained secret key, the user can locally
approximate the value of sT · Ay|y′ for any y ′ . To achieve this, rather than adopting the framework
of Banerjee-Peikert [BP14], we instead follow the approach of Boneh et al. [BLMR13]. The issue
with [BP14] is that it computes Ay using a binary tree structure rather than sequentially. While
it improves concrete efficiency, it is unclear whether the prefix-fixing ideas could be applied there.
On the other hand, evaluation in [BLMR13] proceeds sequentially. In particular, let ℓ be the length
of y, Ay is defined as

                       Ay = Ay[1] · G−1 Ay[2] · G−1 Ay[3] . . . G−1 Ay[ℓ] ,
                                                                             


which allows the key-constraining algorithm to assign a partial key sT · Ay + noisey for arbitrary
lengths of y, after which the user can independently compute the approximate value of sT · Ay|y′ .
By combining the above with the fact that any range constraint (even of exponential size) can be
decomposed into polynomially many prefix checks (using the power-of-two trick), we can give out
constrained keys for arbitrary range predicates efficiently. To illustrate this, consider the following
simple example: let [y, z] be the desired range, where y = 0010 and z = 1011. The key-constraining
algorithm will assign partial keys corresponding to 0012, 0122, and 1022, where 2 denotes a
wildcard position. Using this, the constraining algorithm can generate compute-&-compare -style
constrained keys for differing length targets.
    We highlight that although our collusion-resistant CPRF construction naturally extends our
compute-&-compare CPRF scheme, we are unable to generalize it to prove (full) constraint hiding.
The issue is that, if we rely on a similar homomorphic-encryption-based constraint hiding template,
evaluating f (x) requires explicitly using f to ‘select’ the partial key corresponding to a prefix of
f (x). Thus, the evaluator needs some information about f (x) (which is just the maximum length of
the matching prefix as per above decomposition) in order to correctly evaluate the PRF. However,
we note that if an evaluator gets this additional information, then we can indeed prove constraint
hiding for predicated range circuits. We believe such a weaker notion of constraint hiding might be
useful for certain applications, and we leave the problem of constraint hiding for predicated range
circuits as an interesting open problem.

2.4   Applications to 2-Sided Predicate Encryption
We explore the implications of our construction to 2-sided predicate encryption (PE), contrasting
it with the more common 1-sided variant. In a standard PE scheme [BW07, KSW08], a secret key
skf enables the decryption of a ciphertext associated with attribute x if and only if f (x) = 1. In
the 1-sided setting, attribute-hiding is required only when f (x) = 0. In the 2-sided setting, x must
remain computationally hidden even from a user who possesses a key that successfully decrypts the
ciphertext (i.e., when f (x) = 1). Achieving 2-sided security for general predicates is notoriously
difficult, as it is essentially equivalent to collusion-resistant Functional Encryption [SW05, BW07,
KSW08, BSW11].


                                                  12
    We introduce a refined security notion termed 2-sided purified security. This notion guarantees
attribute-hiding provided that either:
   1. Non-satisfying keys: All queried keys skfi satisfy fi (x) = 0.

   2. Purified satisfying keys: Any queried key skfj that satisfies fj (x) = 1 belongs to a purified
      circuit class (e.g., compute-&-Compare).
Crucially, we do not restrict non-satisfying queries, which may be arbitrary. We demonstrate that
any 1-sided PE scheme (instantiable from LWE [GVW15, GKW17a, WZ17]) can be generically
transformed into a 2-sided purified PE scheme using our collusion-resistant CPRFs.
   To encrypt a message m under attribute x, the encryptor does the following:
   1. Attribute Encapsulation: Computes a symmetric-key encryption of x as ctx ← SKE.Enc(k, x).

   2. Tag Generation: Derives a tag τ ← CPRF.Eval(cprf.msk, ctx ).

   3. 1-Sided Encryption: Encrypts m using a 1-sided PE scheme under the augmented attribute
      (ctx , τ ).
To create a secret key, we first sample a constrained PRF key for a compute-&-compare predicate
(f, y) that decrypts ctx and checks if f (Dec(k, ctx )) = y. Next, we sample a 1-sided PE key that
checks if the CPRF evaluation (using the above constrain key) on the ciphertext matches the tag τ .
Because the message is “shielded” by the CPRF tag, an adversary learns only the bit representing
the success of the evaluation, leaving x hidden even upon successful decryption.
    Our scheme only works in the symmetric-key setting as the encryptor needs to evaluate the
CPRF for obtaining the ‘tag’ in the ciphertext. We leave it as an exciting open problem to generalize
our construction to the public-key setting.

2.5    Discussion and Future Directions
Boosting to Impure Classes. A natural question is whether CPRFs for purified constraints can
serve as a mechanism to bootstrap to more expressive, “impure” classes. While a jump to general
circuits is likely precluded by some complexity theoretic lower bounds, we provide partial positive
results for “weakly impure” constraints in Section 11.
     We define a circuit class C as weakly impure if any C ∈ C can be expressed as a sum of poly(λ)
purified circuits C1 , . . . , Ck from a purified class C ′ . To issue a key for C ∈ C, the authority generates
k independent CPRF keys for the constituent purified circuits. This allows us to handle predicates
with bounded overlaps. For example, consider a range-based class where two keys might overlap
on a small, fixed-length interval. By “purifying” these overlaps during the key-generation phase
(i.e., treating the intersection as its own disjoint sub-predicate) we can extend the utility of our
construction to non-disjoint settings.
Open Question: Towards Arbitrary Purified Constraints. Our work leaves open the chal-
lenge of designing CPRFs for arbitrary purified circuit classes. Specifically, can we construct
collusion-resistant CPRFs for any poly-size constraints where the only guarantee is that their sup-
ports are disjoint?
     An affirmative answer from standard lattice assumptions would be a major breakthrough, as
it would suggest that “zeroizing” attacks are the primary obstacles to collusion resistance. In Sec-
tion 12, we provide a candidate CPRF for log-depth constraints which we conjecture to be secure

                                                      13
under purified corruption. We provide a proof under an extremely strong non-falsifiable lattice
assumption, and pose the formal proof under a falsifiable lattice assumption (or cryptanalysis) of
this candidate as an open problem.

5     Purifying Functionality: CPRFs and PE
In this work, we put forth the concept of purified functionality in functional cryptography. As
discussed earlier, the community currently struggles with designing and proving security of many
cryptographic primitives under general adversarial attack strategies. For instance, prior works in
CPRFs and PE typically only focus on 1-key security. Our contribution is to get around this
shortcoming by proposing a new notion of purification across different cryptographic primitives.
As our main case study, we start with CPRFs and later extend it to PE as well.

5.2   Predicate Encryption for Purified Predicates
Similar to CPRFs, we propose the notion of purified predicates in the context of (secret-key)
predicate encryption. Informally, a purified (secret-key) PE system is defined exactly as a regular
PE system (see Section 4.2), i.e. with same syntax and correctness. As for purified CPRFs, we
define predicate privacy for PE in a similar manner, which is the predicate keys corrupted by an
attacker must correspond to a purified class of predicates (as in Fig. 1).
    However, unlike purified CPRFs, we define the new purified security properties for PE in a
slightly stronger way. A purified PE systems guarantees 2-sided security as long as the attacker
either makes arbitrary unsatisfying predicate queries (i.e., do not require queries to correspond to a
purified circuit class), or if it makes a satisfying predicate query, then all predicates correspond to
a purified circuit class (as in Fig. 1). Thus, a purified PE provides strictly stronger security when
compared to a regular 1-sided predicate encryption system [GKW17b]. We explain it formally
below.

Definition 5.4 (Purified 2-Sided Security). An SK-PE scheme PE is said to be (fully) 2-sided
secure for purified predicates if every admissible PPT adversary A has negligible advantage in the
2-sided security game as defined in Theorem 4.4, where A must satisfy the following additional
admissibility condition: let CA = {Ci }i denote the set of all circuits queried by A to the KeyGen
oracle; if Ci (x0 ) = Ci (x1 ) = 1 for some queried circuit Ci , then CA must be a purified circuit class
as per Eq. (2) for A to be admissible.
    In words, the admissibility condition is only changed for ‘one-side’. That is, the corrupted keys
must correspond to a purified circuit class only when an attacker corrupts at least one satisfying
secret key.

Definition 5.5 (Purified Predicate Privacy). An SK-PE scheme PE is said satisfy predicate pri-
vacy for purified predicates if every admissible PPT adversary A has negligible advantage in the
predicate privacy security game as defined in Theorem 4.5, where A must satisfy the following
additional admissibility condition: let {(Ci,0 , Ci,1 )}i denote the set of circuit-pairs queried by A to
the challenge key-gen oracle Ob and CA,b = {Ci,b }i ; CA,0 and CA,1 must both be purified constrain
classes, individually, as per Eq. (2) for A to be admissible.

    For an admissible challenge input x∗ , let zx∗ denote the CPRF value computed before applying
H. In the ROM proof, the simulator answers the challenge query by a fresh random string and
programs H at zx∗ . This programming is consistent unless the adversary has already queried zx∗
to H, or obtains the same oracle point through another evaluation query. Thus the only bad
events are that the adversary queries zx∗ to H, or finds some evaluation query x ̸= x∗ such that
zx = zx∗ . The first event is ruled out by the underlying hidden-preimage property of the algebraic
construction: for an admissible x∗ , the value zx∗ cannot be computed from the public parameters,
evaluation queries, and admissible constrained keys. The second event is ruled out by the standard
collision argument for the underlying algebraic evaluation map. Hence, conditioned on these bad
events not occurring, the value H(zx∗ ) is unseen by the adversary and is distributed as a fresh
random string. This gives the ROM adaptive-security upgrade via the standard output-hashing
paradigm of [AMN+ 18].

6.2    Purified Constraint Pseudorandomness
Next, we prove that our CPRF satisfies semi-adaptive purified constraint psuedorandomness, where
the attacker can corrupt any polynomials number of constraint keys as long as they correspond
to the compute-&-compare class. (Refer to Section 5.1.) We point out that we only prove semi-
adaptive security, which is identical to as defined Theorem 5.1, except we require the attacker to
specify the function f at the beginning. For completeness, we formally define it below.

(collusion-resistant) semi-adaptive constrained pseudorandomness for compute-&-compare circuits,

for all λ ∈ N, the following holds:

8.2    Purified Constraint Pseudorandomness
We prove that our CPRF satisfies semi-adaptive pseudorandomness security as in Theorem 6.1,
except we also require each input (sent by A during evaluation query) is not a satisfying input for
any constraint that A gets a constrained key for. For simplicity, we still refer to this as semi-adaptive
purified constraint pseudorandomness. The reason this restriction was not needed for compute-&-
compare class is that in compute-&-compare class, the constrained keys generated for answering
the evaluation queries will later be reused for the constrained key query, however in predicated
range class, the challenger cannot predict the range of the constrained key queries and thus cannot
reuse the keys. At a very high level, this issue is very similar to the difficulty of answering secret
key queries in hierarchical and standard IBE [GKR25].

Definition 8.1 (Semi-Adaptive Purified Constrained Pseudorandomness). A CPRF F satisfies
(collusion-resistant) semi-adaptive constrained pseudorandomness for predicated range circuits if
the advantage of any PPT adversary in the experiment described in Theorem 6.1 (generalized to
predicated range constraints) is always negligible, where the adversary must also adhere to the
restriction that each of A’s evaluation query x (and the challenge query x∗ ) must not satisfy the
predicated range constraint for any constrained key query (i.e., f (x) ∈

In this section, we design predicate encryption for compute-&-compare circuits of the purified
class. And our design can also be generalized to the predicated range class. Our design relies on
constrained PRF for compute-&-compare (CPRF.Setup, CPRF.Eval, CPRF.Constrain, CPRF.CEval),
secret key encryption scheme (SKE.Setup, SKE.Enc, SKE.Dec), and 1-sided secret key predicate en-
cryption (PE.Setup, PE.Enc, PE.KeyGen, PE.Dec).

11.1        Further discussion: beyond CPRFs, constraint hiding, and more
The above principle of bootstrapping cryptographic primitives to beyond purified classes is ex-
tremely general, thus could be applied in the context of predicate encryption, functional encryption,
and more. However, such generic compilers do not carry forward the predicate privacy property
(such as constraint privacy, function hiding, etc). The reason is that during the above compilation
process we must give out the constraint circuit in the clear (for ensuring correctness). Thus, even
when the underlying CPRFs satisfy constraint privacy, our resulting CPRFs for weakly impure
circuits do not satisfy constraint privacy. It is an interesting question whether we can either gener-
ically, or even in a non-black-box way, get around this limitation. This is an interesting question
for future research.
    Additionally, our current bootstrapping approach clearly relies on decomposing a given impure
circuit into a sequence of pure circuits, and then doing an independent key generation for each
purified circuit. We believe one needs to take advantage of the fact that the key generation algo-
rithm gets complete access to circuit and not just each purified sub-component to ensure we could
bootstrap to more general circuits.
    Finally, it is an interesting question whether our approach of starting from purified circuits can
be further used in other areas of cryptography to derive more meaningful results.
